passages.t: ‘The head of every man is Christ’: heads and coverings
passages.happening:
Paul ends the long answer about food with one line: “You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ” (verse 1).

Then he turns to the church's worship. He praises them for keeping the teachings he passed on (verse 2). “But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God” (verse 3).

“Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head” (verse 4). “And every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, for it is just as if her head were shaved” (verse 5). If a woman will not cover her head, she might as well cut her hair off; and if that is shameful, “she should cover her head” (verse 6).

This passage is one of the most debated in all of Paul's letters. The book page lists it among the letter's hard passages. These notes say what Paul says, what can and cannot be known about the setting, and how churches read it, without taking a side.
passages.hearers:
Notice first who is speaking in the church. Paul expects both men and women to pray and to prophesy, which means to speak a message from God aloud for others to hear. He does not tell the women to stop. He tells them how to do it. Joel had promised that “Your sons and daughters will prophesy” (Joel 2:28), and Peter said that promise came true at Pentecost (Acts 2:17).

‘Head’ is used in two ways at once. Each person has a physical head, and each has a ‘head’ in the sense of verse 3. To dishonour your own head may mean both: to bring shame on yourself, and on the one who is your head.

What did a covered head mean in Roman Corinth? Some of it is known and much is disputed. Roman men, when they offered sacrifice or prayed in public rites, often drew a fold of the toga over the head. Many statues show emperors and other men praying or sacrificing that way. Corinth was a Roman colony. So a man praying with his head covered may have looked like a Roman priest or a man of rank at a pagan rite. That is one likely reason for verse 4, though scholars debate it.

For women, many scholars think that respectable married women in the Roman world usually covered their heads in public, as a sign of modesty and of being married. Others think the evidence is more mixed than that. Paul does not use the usual Greek word for a veil, and some readers think the ‘covering’ is a matter of hair: long hair worn up, not loose.

A shaved head (verse 5) was shameful for a woman. Paul uses that shame as his comparison. The point seems to be that a woman praying uncovered would bring the same shame on herself and her household that a shaved head would.
passages.ot:
In Israel's Scriptures ‘head’ could mean the one at the top: “The LORD will make you the head and not the tail” (Deuteronomy 28:13). It could also be used of where a river begins. The river from Eden “branched into four headwaters” (Genesis 2:10), where the Hebrew word is the word for heads.

Hair and covering had meanings in Israel too. In the test for a wife accused of unfaithfulness, the priest “is to let down her hair” (Numbers 5:18), a sign of shame. A man under a Nazirite vow, set apart to God, “must let the hair of his head grow long” (Numbers 6:5). And the priests were told, “They must not shave their heads or let their hair grow long, but must carefully trim their hair” (Ezekiel 44:20). So the way the head was worn in worship was not a small thing in the Old Testament either.
passages.hard:
What does ‘head’ (Greek kephalē) mean in verse 3?

Readers give three main answers. Many take it to mean authority: Christ has authority over every man, a husband over his wife, and God over Christ. Others take it to mean source or origin, as the head of a river is its source: man came from Christ the Creator, woman came from man (verse 8, Genesis 2:22), and Christ came from God. Others take it to mean the one who is most prominent or honoured, the one who stands for the rest. Scholars have argued over the Greek evidence for each sense for decades, and many think more than one sense is at work.

‘The head of Christ is God’ does not make Christ less than God. The church confesses that the Son is fully God with the Father. Many read this line of the Son's willing obedience to the Father as the one sent.

From these readings Christians draw different conclusions, and these notes do not choose.

Complementarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth before God, and that God has given them different roles in the church and the home, with the office of pastor or elder, and teaching the gathered church with that authority, given to qualified men. Many of them read verse 3 as an order of authority set in creation, and they gladly note that the same passage has women praying and prophesying.

Egalitarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth and that every role in the church, including pastor and teacher, is open to both, as God gifts them. Many of them read ‘head’ as source, and point to verses 11 and 12, where Paul says that in the Lord man and woman depend on each other.

Both sides agree that women and men are made in God's image and that both prayed and prophesied in Paul's churches.
passages.asks: Paul cared that worship did not bring shame on anyone or blur what God made. Ask whether anything in how you take part in worship draws attention to yourself or dishonours others. And whatever your church's practice, ask how you can honour both the men and the women who serve God beside you.

passages.happening:
Paul gives reasons. A man should not cover his head, “since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man” (verse 7). Woman came from man, and was created for man (verses 8-9). “For this reason a woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head, because of the angels” (verse 10).

Then he balances it. “In the Lord, however, woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman” (verse 11). “For just as woman came from man, so also man is born of woman. But everything comes from God” (verse 12).

He asks them to judge for themselves whether it is proper for a woman to pray to God uncovered (verse 13). “Doesn’t nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a disgrace to him, but that if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For long hair is given to her as a covering” (verses 14-15).

“If anyone is inclined to dispute this, we have no other practice, nor do the churches of God” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
‘Glory’ in this world of honour and shame meant the one who brings honour to another. Paul says man shows God's honour, and woman shows man's. He does not say woman is not made in God's image. Genesis says both are.

Verse 10 is hard even in Greek. It says a woman ought to have ‘authority on her head’. The words ‘a sign of’ are added by translators. Some take the authority to be a sign that she is under her husband's authority. Others take it as her own authority: the covering marks her right to pray and prophesy in the church.

‘Because of the angels’ is one of the most puzzling phrases in the letter. No one is sure what Paul meant. Many think of angels present when the church worships, who care about order in God's house. Some think of the angels who sinned in Genesis 6. Others have other ideas. These notes say plainly that it is uncertain.

Verses 11 and 12 matter a great deal. ‘In the Lord’ means in the new life of those who belong to Christ. There, Paul says, neither man nor woman stands alone. The first woman came from the first man, but every man since has come from a woman. And everything comes from God. Whatever Paul has said about order, he will not let it become a claim that men need women less, or count for more.

‘Nature’ in verse 14 probably means the way things are usually done and felt, what seems natural, more than biology. In Paul's world men usually wore their hair short and women long. In verse 15 the Greek says long hair is given ‘as’ or ‘instead of’ a covering, and some readers think that means the hair itself is the covering Paul has in mind.

Verse 16 appeals to what all the churches do. Paul does not want Corinth to go its own way.
passages.ot:
Paul's argument rests on Genesis. “So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). Both man and woman bear God's image.

Genesis 2 tells the second account. “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper” (Genesis 2:18). The word ‘helper’ does not mean a lesser person. Moses used the same word of God: “The God of my father was my helper” (Exodus 18:4). God made the woman from the man's side, and the man said, “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23). Paul's ‘woman came from man’ (verse 8) points here. His ‘man is born of woman’ (verse 12) points to every birth since.
passages.hard:
How should churches apply this passage today? Faithful churches answer in different ways, and these notes do not choose.

Some churches keep the practice of covering. Among them are many Amish and conservative Mennonite communities, where women wear a covering, and many Plymouth Brethren assemblies, where women cover their heads in the meetings. They hold that Paul grounds the practice in creation and in ‘the angels’, not only in custom, and that ‘the churches of God’ (verse 16) means it is for every church. The Catholic Church's law of 1917 asked women to cover their heads in church; the law of 1983 has no such rule, and some Catholic women still choose to.

Most churches today read the covering as the sign of a lasting principle in a form that belonged to its culture. On this view what remains is that men and women honour God and each other in worship, and do not throw off what marked honour and modesty in their own setting. Others read verse 15 to mean the covering is the hair itself, so the passage is about hair.

Two more things should be said. First, this passage has women praying and prophesying aloud. In chapter 14 Paul writes, “Women are to be silent in the churches” (14:34). The two cannot mean that women must say nothing at all. The notes on chapter 14 set out how readers fit them together.

Second, nothing here lowers women's worth or gives anyone the right to treat women with contempt. Nor should any church despise another over this question, whether it covers or not. Paul's last word before his appeal to the churches was that man and woman need each other, and everything comes from God.
passages.asks: Paul's argument ends in mutual need: man and woman, neither without the other. Ask where you have acted as if you did not need someone God has placed beside you. And if your church differs from another on this passage, ask how you can hold your view without looking down on theirs.

passages.t: ‘It is not the Lord’s Supper you eat’
passages.happening:
Now Paul has no praise. “In the following instructions I have no praise to offer, because your gatherings do more harm than good” (verse 17).

He has heard that when they meet as a church, there are divisions, “and in part I believe it” (verse 18). Such differences show who is truly approved (verse 19).

“Now then, when you come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat” (verse 20). “For as you eat, each of you goes ahead without sharing his meal. While one remains hungry, another gets drunk” (verse 21).

“Don’t you have your own homes in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What can I say to you? Shall I praise you for this? No, I will not!” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
In Paul's day the Lord's Supper was part of a real meal. The church met in homes, often the house of a believer with some wealth, since there were no church buildings. They ate together, and the bread and cup belonged to that meal.

A well-off Roman house had a formal dining room, where guests lay on couches to eat, leaning on one elbow. It held only a few. Others could gather in a larger hall or courtyard. One scholar compared the floor plans of several houses found at Corinth and elsewhere and judged that not everyone in a church could have reclined in the dining room. Roman dinner customs openly ranked guests: the host's friends and equals might lie in the dining room and get better food and wine, while others were served elsewhere and less.

Many scholars think that pattern explains verse 21. The wealthy, free to arrive early, began their meal and ate and drank well. Slaves and labourers, who could only come after work, arrived to find little or nothing left. Each went ahead with ‘his own’ meal. The meal that should have shown one family showed the city's ranks instead.

So Paul's anger is not about manners. To ‘humiliate those who have nothing’ was to shame them in front of everyone, in a world where honour and shame meant almost everything. And to do that, Paul says, is to ‘despise the church of God’.
passages.ot:
The Law and the Prophets are full of God's care for the poor at the table. Moses told Israel that when a brother is poor, “you are not to harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother” (Deuteronomy 15:7). Isaiah describes the worship God wants: “to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home” (Isaiah 58:7). And Proverbs says, “Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him” (Proverbs 14:31).

Jesus taught the same at a dinner: “But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind” (Luke 14:13).
passages.asks: At Corinth the Lord's table had become a place where some felt at home and others felt shamed. Ask who might feel like that in your church: the poor, the newcomer, the person who does not fit. Then ask what it would take for them to find a place at the table, not just what is left over.

passages.t: ‘This is My body, which is for you’
passages.happening:
Paul reminds them where the Supper came from. “For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you: The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread, and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, ‘This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me’” (verses 23-24).

“In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me’” (verse 25).

“For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
These verses are the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper that we have. 1 Corinthians was probably written in the mid-50s, and most scholars think the Gospels were written down later. So this is older, as writing, than the accounts in Matthew, Mark and Luke.

And Paul says it was older still. ‘Received’ and ‘passed on’ are the words for handing on a teaching faithfully, from teacher to student. Paul had passed this on to the Corinthians when he founded the church, a few years before. He says he received it ‘from the Lord’: it comes from Jesus himself, through those who were there.

Paul's words are very close to Luke's: “This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me” (Luke 22:19), and the cup ‘after supper’ (Luke 22:20). Paul and Luke travelled together.

Notice ‘on the night He was betrayed’. Jesus gave this meal to friends who would fail him that very night. And ‘after supper’ shows that the bread and the cup belonged to a whole meal.

‘Remembrance’ is anamnēsis. In Israel's worship, to remember was more than to recall. At Passover each generation remembered the rescue from Egypt as its own. To remember Christ at the Supper is to bring his death into the present life of the church.

Verse 26 says the meal itself preaches. Every time the church eats and drinks, it ‘proclaims’ the Lord's death. And it looks ahead: ‘until He comes’.
passages.ot:
The Supper grew out of the Passover. Of that night God said, “And this day will be a memorial for you, and you are to celebrate it as a feast to the LORD” (Exodus 12:14).

‘The new covenant in My blood’ points to two Old Testament passages. At Sinai, Moses sprinkled blood on the people and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you” (Exodus 24:8). And through Jeremiah God promised something new: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” (Jeremiah 31:31). In it, “I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). Jesus says that covenant is made in his blood.
passages.hard:
What does ‘This is My body’ mean? Christians have read these words in different ways, and the disagreement is old and serious. Here is how each church describes its own belief.

The Catholic Church teaches that at the consecration the whole substance of the bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ, while the appearance of bread and wine remains. Its Catechism says this change is fittingly and properly called transubstantiation.

The Orthodox churches also believe that the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. Most prefer to call the change a holy mystery and do not try to explain how it happens.

Lutherans teach that Christ's true body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine.

Reformed and Presbyterian churches teach that Christ is truly present by his Spirit, and that those who receive in faith spiritually feed on Christ crucified and all the benefits of his death. The Westminster Confession says this feeding is real, but spiritual, not bodily.

Many Baptists, and others in free churches, hold that the Supper is chiefly a memorial: an act of remembering Christ's death as he commanded, of proclaiming it, and of sharing as one body.

These notes do not settle the question. Every one of these churches agrees that Jesus gave this meal to his followers, that it points to his death for them, and that it looks ahead to the kingdom.
passages.asks: Jesus gave this meal to people who would fail him that very night. Ask whether you come to it as someone who has earned a place, or as someone being given one. And notice ‘until He comes’: ask what it would mean to eat the next time as someone waiting for him.

passages.t: ‘In an unworthy manner’, and ‘wait for one another’
passages.happening:
“Therefore, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord” (verse 27).

“Each one must examine himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup” (verse 28). “For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself” (verse 29).

“That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a number of you have fallen asleep” (verse 30).

If we judged ourselves rightly, we would not come under judgment (verse 31). “But when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world” (verse 32).

“So, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another” (verse 33). The hungry should eat at home first, so that their gathering does not bring judgment (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
‘In an unworthy manner’ is one word in Greek, anaxiōs, ‘unworthily’. It describes how a person eats, not what kind of person is eating. In this chapter the unworthy manner is plain: eating ahead, getting drunk, and shaming the poor at the Lord's own table (verses 21-22).

‘Without recognizing the body’ (verse 29) uses a verb, diakrinō, that means to discern or tell apart. Some take ‘the body’ to be Christ's body given for us, which the bread shows. Others take it to be the church, the body of Christ that the wealthy were despising (10:17; 12:27). Many think Paul means both: to despise the church at the table is to despise the Christ who gave his body for it.

‘Fallen asleep’ is the early Christians' gentle word for believers who have died. Paul says plainly that some in Corinth were weak, some were sick and some had died, and he says it was God's judgment on how they treated the Supper.

But he calls it discipline, the correction a father gives his children, ‘so that we will not be condemned with the world’. The judgment is meant to save, not to destroy.

The remedy is simple and practical. ‘Wait for one another.’ Share the meal. Let no one go hungry while others feast.
passages.ot:
Israel knew that coming before God carelessly was dangerous. Yet the Old Testament also shows God disciplining his people as a father. “As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him. For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust” (Psalm 103:13-14). Hebrews quotes Proverbs: “For the Lord disciplines the one He loves” (Hebrews 12:6).

The prophets judged the rich who ignored the poor. Amos condemned those who “trample on the heads of the poor as on the dust of the earth” (Amos 2:7).
passages.hard:
Does ‘in an unworthy manner’ mean only sinless people may come to the table?

No. In context the unworthy manner is the way the Corinthians ate: despising the poor and treating the meal as their own private dinner. No one is worthy of the Supper in the sense of deserving it. It was given to sinners, on the night Jesus was betrayed. ‘Examine himself’ means to look honestly at how you come, and how you are treating the rest of the body, and then to eat. Paul says ‘examine’ and then ‘eat’, not ‘examine’ and stay away.

What about verse 30? Paul says that God judged the church in Corinth with sickness and death for how they abused the Supper. These notes do not soften that. It is a sober word. But Paul could say it because he was an apostle writing to a church he knew. It does not give anyone today the right to say that a person's illness or death was God's punishment for how they took the Supper. Jesus warned against reading suffering that way (John 9:2-3). No one should be told that.

If you are afraid to come to the table because you fear you are not good enough, or that you will eat judgment on yourself, notice who this warning was for: people who were shaming the poor and getting drunk at the meal. A tender conscience that worries about coming is far from them. Jesus said, “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (John 6:37). Talk with your pastor about your fear.

Who may come to the table? Churches differ: some invite all who trust in Christ, some ask that those who come be baptized or be members of a church of the same faith, and these notes do not settle it.
passages.asks: Paul's answer to a deep problem was simple: wait for one another. Ask who you might be ‘going ahead of’ in your church: in food, in welcome, in attention. And before you next come to the table, ask how you are treating the body, Christ's people, as well as how you are receiving his body given for you.
